note: The exclusion register (PLAN.md §3). Every tempting parallel that was considered and rejected, with the reason. A catalogue that only records what it accepted cannot be checked; this file is what makes the accepted set falsifiable. Machine candidates that were never plausible are not all listed individually — see `formulaic` batches, which name the shared string and the verses it drew.

categories.wrong-sense: The string matches but the meaning is opposed or unrelated; the parallel is an artifact of English word order.
categories.formulaic: The shared words are KJV connective or narrative boilerplate ('and it came to pass', 'unto them concerning the') that the Book of Mormon uses continuously and that carry no intertextual signal.
categories.common-vocabulary: The shared words are real content words but too widely distributed in the KJV to point at any one verse.
categories.better-source-identified: A genuine link exists at this verse, but to a different source; the rejected candidate is superseded.
categories.insufficient-verbal: A conceptual resemblance with too little verbal contact to adjudicate as a link at any confidence.

exclusions.reason: A four-word run of pure connective tissue. Acts 7:44 concerns the tabernacle's pattern and shares no content word with Nephi's colophon.
Connective boilerplate; Ezekiel's subject is priestly adjudication of controversies.
Four words of connective phrasing spanning a clause boundary in both texts.
Temporal connective. The following noun differs ('year' vs 'hour').

'And/wherefore it came to pass' is the Book of Mormon's single most frequent narrative connective and occurs hundreds of times in the KJV. It should never be treated as evidence of dependence on any particular verse, and candidates resting on it alone are excluded throughout this catalogue without further comment.
A standard KJV formula for prayer with no distinctive content. The real link at this verse is to the Exodus pillar-of-fire theophany; see the accepted link.
Ordinary narrative motion. Absalom's return to his own house has no thematic contact with Lehi's.
Locative boilerplate; the shared string straddles a clause boundary.
A locative phrase. Joshua 10:13 concerns the sun standing still, not a descending figure.
Three content-free words plus 'sun'; Deuteronomy's subject is the hour of the passover sacrifice.
'Filled with' takes wisdom, the Spirit, fury, and much else across the KJV. Hiram of Tyre being filled with craftsman's wisdom is not a source for Lehi being filled with the Spirit.
A stock phrase of prophetic judgement distributed across the KJV; Jeremiah alone offers many closer contexts. Nothing points to Job.
Connective boilerplate spanning a clause boundary.
The shared string is an accident of the Book of Mormon's 'such as' introducing a quotation and Jeremiah's 'such as are for death'. Different constructions entirely.
Boilerplate; Leviticus concerns the meat offering.
Four function words.

A temporal connective. Scored relatively high (1.50) because the five-word run is uncommon, which illustrates that n-gram rarity tracks string frequency and not significance: rare boilerplate is still boilerplate.
Ordinary narrative motion.

This is the most instructive rejection in the chapter. Proverbs 12:10 gave the longest contiguous match in the machine's candidate set for this verse — five words, scoring 2.00 — and it is wrong. The Proverbs verse reads 'the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel': the phrase is there to be negated, and its subject is the opposite of Nephi's. The true source, Psalm 145:9 ('his tender mercies are over all his works'), shares fewer contiguous words and so never surfaced in the n-gram stream at all, but supplies both halves of Nephi's sentence — the subject 'tender mercies' and the predicate 'over all', a pairing found in no other KJV verse. A longer string match is not a better one, and the contiguous-window method is structurally blind to sources whose agreement is split across a clause.

A four-word run of announcement formula. Worth noting for a different reason, however: the 1830 text spells it 'shew', exactly as the KJV does, and the 1920 edition modernized it to 'show'. The orthography is evidence about the Book of Mormon's relation to KJV English generally, and belongs in the variant register rather than here as a link to any particular verse.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that the LORD spake unto
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and worthless. 'And it came to pass that the Lord spake unto' is the Book of Mormon's standard narrative hinge and appears three times in this chapter alone (2:1, 2:2, 2:19); Joshua 1:1 shares it because both texts are King James narrative prose. Recorded here once, at length, as the model case for why n-gram run length is a recall floor and not a ranking (CONVENTIONS.md §9); the same match at 2:2 and 2:19 is passed over in silence.
Connective. Abiathar's banishment shares no content word with the Lord's commendation of Lehi, and the causal 'because thou hast been' is ordinary KJV subordination.
Four words spanning a clause boundary; Numbers 36:2 concerns the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters.

The renunciation list at 2:4 is real, but its Gospel source is the hundredfold saying (Matthew 19:29 and parallels), which supplies houses AND lands AND the promised inheritance. Mark 13:34's householder leaves his house to travel and gives his servants authority — the departure is a parable frame, not a renunciation. Superseded.
Joseph leaves his garment in Potiphar's wife's hand. Shared words are the verb and two pronouns.
Abigail riding down a hill. Pure motion idiom.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when he had
exclusions.reason: Another long run of narrative hinge; see the Joshua 1:1 entry at 2:1. Ezekiel's subject is the man in linen taking fire from between the cherubim.

The Red Sea link in this chapter is carried at 2:5 by the unique phrase 'the shore of the Red sea' (1 Kings 9:26) and at 2:6 by 'three days in the wilderness' (Exodus 15:22). Exodus 10:19, where the west wind casts the locusts into the Red Sea, contributes nothing the geography does not already supply.

Not a machine candidate, but the parallel a reader reaches for first: 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.' The river-and-righteousness figure is Amos's most famous sentence and it is the wrong source here. Lehi's blessing has the wish-formula ('O that thou'), the commandments in the very next verse, and the river and righteousness together — all four of which are Isaiah 48:18 and only two of which are Amos. The decisive fact is external to the wording: Nephi transcribes Isaiah 48 entire at 1 Nephi 20, so the verse Lehi is using is a verse the book will quote.

'Being filled with the fruits of righteousness' shares a participial formula and nothing else. The source of 2:14 is Micah 3:8, the KJV's only verse joining power to the spirit, and it also supplies the prophetic-rebuke setting Philippians lacks.
Four words of which three are function words; the match breaks at 'his wrath' / 'the valley of Lemuel'.
Spans a clause boundary in both texts; 1 Kings 2:29 reports Joab fled to the tabernacle.
Four function words. One of the commonest strings in the KJV.

The senses are opposed, and instructively so. Luke 21:24 is the destruction of Jerusalem: 'they shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations.' 1 Nephi 2:20 is the promise that answers that destruction: 'shall be led to a land of promise.' The identical four words carry exile in one text and inheritance in the other, and the passive participle is doing opposite work either side. Worth recording because chapter 1 has already used the KJV's exile vocabulary in earnest at 1:13 ('carried away captive into Babylon'), so a reader tracking that thread has real reason to hear it again here — and should not.

A five-word run and a genuine parallel of form: John 15:10 is also a conditional promise turning on commandment-keeping. But the apodosis decides it. John's is abiding in love; 1 Nephi's is prospering in a land, which is the Deuteronomic conditional of 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7 and becomes the Book of Mormon's covenant formula. The Johannine phrasing is a coincidence of the protasis.

'Cut off' is the Pentateuch's standing penalty formula and occurs scores of times; Leviticus 20:17 is one instance among many. What identifies the source at 2:21 is not 'cut off' but 'from the presence of the Lord', which the KJV has in eight verses and which Genesis 4:16 makes a sentence on a brother.
Four words across a clause boundary. Note that Ezekiel 20 IS relevant to this chapter, but at 2:20 (verses 6 and 15, 'the glory of all lands'), not here.
Jehoshaphat's heart lifted up in the ways of the LORD. The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'the ways of remembrance', which is not a KJV construction at all.

Recorded not as a rejection but as the losing half of a mediation test, because the reasoning is the point. Exodus 2:14 is the ultimate source of the formula behind 'a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren' — but the KJV renders it 'a prince and a judge', and only Acts 7:27 and 7:35 render it 'a ruler and a judge'. The Book of Mormon has 'ruler'. So the Old Testament verse is the source of the story and the New Testament verses are the source of the English, which is exactly what the mediation field 'OT-via-NT' exists to record. Exodus 2:14 is carried in the link's composite list.
